lessons.title: Basics (Variables & Types)
lessons.summary: Variables store data. Python is dynamically typed — you don't declare the type, Python figures it out from the value you assign.

learn_cards.title: Variables
learn_cards.body: Variables store data. Python is dynamically typed — you don't declare the type, Python figures it out from the value you assign.

learn_cards.code:
name = "Aniketh"
age = 25
pi = 3.14
is_learning = True
learn_cards.output: # No output — variables are just stored in memory

learn_cards.code:
print(type(42))
print(type("hello"))
print(type(3.14))
print(type(True))

learn_cards.title: Key Insight
learn_cards.body: Everything in Python is an object. Even 42 is an object of type int. You can call methods on it: (42).bit_length() returns 6.

learn_cards.title: f-strings
learn_cards.body: Prefix a string with 'f' to embed expressions inside {curly braces}. This is the modern, preferred way to format strings in Python 3.6+.

learn_cards.code:
name = "Aniketh"
age = 25
print(f"Hi, I'm {name} and I'm {age} years old.")
print(f"Next year I'll be {age + 1}.")
print(f"Pi to 2 decimals: {3.14159:.2f}")
learn_cards.output:
Hi, I'm Aniketh and I'm 25 years old.
Next year I'll be 26.
Pi to 2 decimals: 3.14

learn_cards.title: input()
learn_cards.body: input() reads text from the user. It ALWAYS returns a string, so you need to convert it with int() or float() for numbers.

learn_cards.code:
name = input("What is your name? ")
print(f"Hello, {name}!")

age = int(input("How old are you? "))
print(f"In 10 years you will be {age + 10}.")
learn_cards.output:
What is your name? Aniketh
Hello, Aniketh!
How old are you? 25
In 10 years you will be 35.

lessons.title: Control Flow (if/else, loops)
lessons.summary: Conditional statements let your code make decisions. Python uses indentation (4 spaces) to define blocks — no curly braces needed.

learn_cards.title: if / elif / else
learn_cards.body: Conditional statements let your code make decisions. Python uses indentation (4 spaces) to define blocks — no curly braces needed.

learn_cards.code:
# Comparison: ==  !=  >  <  >=  <=
print(5 == 5)    # True
print(5 != 3)    # True

# Logical: and, or, not
print(True and False)   # False
print(True or False)    # True
print(not True)         # False

# Chaining
x = 5
print(1 < x < 10)  # True — Python supports chaining!
learn_cards.output:
True
True
False
True
False
True

learn_cards.title: for loop
learn_cards.body: Iterates over a sequence (list, string, range, etc). Think of it as: 'for each item in this collection, do something.'

learn_cards.code:
# Iterate over a list
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
for fruit in fruits:
    print(fruit)

# Iterate over a string
for char in "Hi":
    print(char)

# range(stop) — 0 to stop-1
for i in range(5):
    print(i, end=" ")
print()

# range(start, stop)
for i in range(2, 6):
    print(i, end=" ")
print()

# range(start, stop, step)
for i in range(0, 10, 2):
    print(i, end=" ")

learn_cards.title: while loop
learn_cards.body: Keeps running as long as the condition is True. Be careful — if the condition never becomes False, you get an infinite loop!

learn_cards.code:
count = 0
while count < 3:
    print(f"count is {count}")
    count += 1  # Don't forget to update!
learn_cards.output:
count is 0
count is 1
count is 2

lessons.title: Functions (def, *args, lambda)
lessons.summary: A reusable block of code that takes input (arguments), does something, and optionally returns output. Functions help you avoid repeating code and organize logic into named, testable pieces.

learn_cards.title: What is a function?
learn_cards.body: A reusable block of code that takes input (arguments), does something, and optionally returns output. Functions help you avoid repeating code and organize logic into named, testable pieces.

learn_cards.code:
def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

message = greet("Aniketh")
print(message)

def power(base, exponent=2):
    return base ** exponent

print(power(3))       # Uses default exponent=2
print(power(3, 3))    # Overrides to exponent=3
print(power(base=5, exponent=4))  # Keyword arguments

learn_cards.title: Tuple unpacking
learn_cards.body: Python functions can return multiple values as a tuple. You can unpack them into separate variables.

learn_cards.code:
def divide(a, b):
    quotient = a // b
    remainder = a % b
    return quotient, remainder

q, r = divide(17, 5)
print(f"17 / 5 = {q} remainder {r}")

lessons.title: Data Structures (list, dict, set)
lessons.summary: Lists are the workhorse of Python. They're ordered, mutable (you can change them), and can hold any mix of types. Created with square brackets [].
checkpoint_titles: Slicing — Extracting Parts of a List

learn_cards.title: Lists
learn_cards.body: Lists are the workhorse of Python. They're ordered, mutable (you can change them), and can hold any mix of types. Created with square brackets [].

learn_cards.code:
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

# Access by index (0-based)
print(nums[0])     # 10
print(nums[-1])    # 50 (last item)

# Modify
nums[1] = 99
print(nums)        # [10, 99, 30, 40, 50]

# Common methods
nums.append(60)    # Add to end
nums.insert(0, 5)  # Insert at index 0
nums.pop()         # Remove last
print(len(nums))   # Length

learn_cards.title: Slicing — Extracting Parts of a List
Slicing syntax: list[start:stop:step]
learn_cards.body: start is inclusive, stop is exclusive. Omit start for beginning, omit stop for end. Negative indices count from the end.

learn_cards.title: Tuples
learn_cards.body: Like lists but IMMUTABLE — once created, you can't change them. Use tuples for data that shouldn't change (coordinates, RGB colors, etc).

learn_cards.code:
point = (3, 4)
print(point[0])      # 3

# Unpacking
x, y = point
print(f"x={x}, y={y}")

# Tuples as dict keys (lists can't be!)
locations = {(0, 0): "origin", (1, 2): "point A"}
print(locations[(0, 0)])

learn_cards.title: Dictionaries
learn_cards.body: Store data as key-value pairs. Keys must be immutable (strings, numbers, tuples). O(1) average lookup time — very fast!

learn_cards.code:
person = {"name": "Aniketh", "age": 25, "role": "Engineer"}

print(person["name"])          # Aniketh
person["city"] = "NYC"         # Add new key
print(person.get("salary", 0)) # 0 (safe access with default)

# Iterate
for key, value in person.items():
    print(f"  {key}: {value}")
learn_cards.output:
Aniketh
0
  name: Aniketh
  age: 25
  role: Engineer
  city: NYC

lessons.title: OOP (classes, inheritance)
lessons.summary: OOP organizes code around 'objects' that bundle data (attributes) and behavior (methods). A class is the blueprint, an object is the instance. Think of a class as a cookie cutter and objects as cookies.

learn_cards.title: What is OOP?
learn_cards.body: OOP organizes code around 'objects' that bundle data (attributes) and behavior (methods). A class is the blueprint, an object is the instance. Think of a class as a cookie cutter and objects as cookies.

learn_cards.code:
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        self.name = name      # instance attribute
        self.breed = breed

    def bark(self):           # instance method
        return f"{self.name} says Woof!"

my_dog = Dog("Rex", "Labrador")
print(my_dog.bark())
print(f"{my_dog.name} is a {my_dog.breed}")
learn_cards.output:
Rex says Woof!
Rex is a Labrador

learn_cards.title: __init__ and self
learn_cards.body: __init__ is the constructor — called when you create an object. 'self' refers to the instance being created. Every method gets 'self' as its first parameter automatically.

learn_cards.code:
class Counter:
    count = 0  # Class attribute — shared by all instances

    def __init__(self):
        Counter.count += 1  # Modify via class name
        self.id = Counter.count  # Instance attribute

a = Counter()
b = Counter()
c = Counter()
print(f"Total counters: {Counter.count}")  # 3
print(f"c.id = {c.id}")                    # 3

learn_cards.title: Inheritance
learn_cards.body: A child class inherits all attributes and methods from a parent class, then can add or override them. This promotes code reuse.

learn_cards.output:
Whiskers says Meow!
Rex says Woof!

learn_cards.title: Dunder methods
learn_cards.body: Methods with double underscores like __str__, __repr__, __len__, __eq__. They let your objects work with Python's built-in operations.

learn_cards.code:
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __str__(self):       # print() uses this
        return f"Point({self.x}, {self.y})"

    def __repr__(self):      # Debug representation
        return f"Point(x={self.x}, y={self.y})"

    def __eq__(self, other):  # == comparison
        return self.x == other.x and self.y == other.y

    def __add__(self, other):  # + operator
        return Point(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y)

p1 = Point(1, 2)
p2 = Point(3, 4)
print(p1)            # Uses __str__
print(p1 + p2)       # Uses __add__
print(p1 == Point(1, 2))  # Uses __eq__

lessons.title: Hash Maps (hashing, dicts deep dive)
lessons.summary: A hash map (dict in Python) stores key-value pairs using a hash function to compute an index into an internal array. This gives O(1) average lookup, insert, and delete — much faster than searching a list.
checkpoint_titles: Custom Hashable Objects as Dict Keys

learn_cards.title: What is a Hash Map?
learn_cards.body: A hash map (dict in Python) stores key-value pairs using a hash function to compute an index into an internal array. This gives O(1) average lookup, insert, and delete — much faster than searching a list.

learn_cards.code:
print(hash("hello"))      # Some integer
print(hash(42))           # 42 (ints hash to themselves for small values)
print(hash((1, 2, 3)))    # Tuples are hashable

# Lists are NOT hashable (mutable = unhashable)
# hash([1, 2, 3])  # TypeError!
learn_cards.output: hash values vary by run, but you'll see integers

learn_cards.title: Hashable = Immutable
learn_cards.body: Only immutable objects can be hashed: str, int, float, tuple, frozenset. Mutable objects (list, dict, set) CANNOT be dictionary keys.

learn_cards.title: Internal structure
learn_cards.body: Python's dict uses an open-addressing hash table. When you do d['key'], Python: (1) computes hash('key'), (2) uses the hash to find a slot in an internal array, (3) handles collisions by probing nearby slots. Since Python 3.7, dicts preserve insertion order.

learn_cards.code:
# Building a dict step by step
d = {}
d["name"] = "Aniketh"  # hash("name") -> slot -> store
d["age"] = 25          # hash("age") -> slot -> store
d["role"] = "Engineer" # hash("role") -> slot -> store

# All O(1) lookups
print(d["name"])   # Direct hash lookup, no scanning
print(len(d))      # 3

learn_cards.title: Collisions
learn_cards.body: When two different keys hash to the same slot, it's a collision. Python handles this with open addressing (probing the next available slot). Good hash functions minimize collisions.

learn_cards.code:
# Python handles collisions transparently
# Even if two keys collide, both are stored correctly
d = {}
for i in range(1000):
    d[f"key_{i}"] = i
print(f"Stored {len(d)} items without any issues")
print(f"Lookup: d['key_500'] = {d['key_500']}")
learn_cards.output:
Stored 1000 items without any issues
Lookup: d['key_500'] = 500

learn_cards.title: OrderedDict
learn_cards.body: Since Python 3.7, regular dicts preserve insertion order. So when do you need OrderedDict? Two cases: (1) when equality comparison should consider order, (2) when you need move_to_end().

lessons.title: Comprehensions & Generators
lessons.summary: Comprehensions are Python's elegant, concise syntax for creating collections. They replace multi-line for loops with a single readable line. Python has list, dict, set, and generator comprehensions.

learn_cards.title: Comprehensions
learn_cards.body: Comprehensions are Python's elegant, concise syntax for creating collections. They replace multi-line for loops with a single readable line. Python has list, dict, set, and generator comprehensions.

learn_cards.code:
# Without comprehension
squares = []
for x in range(6):
    squares.append(x ** 2)
print(squares)

# With comprehension — same result, one line
squares = [x ** 2 for x in range(6)]
print(squares)

# Only even squares
even_squares = [x**2 for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]
print(even_squares)

# if-else inside the expression (not the filter)
labels = ["even" if x % 2 == 0 else "odd" for x in range(5)]
print(labels)

learn_cards.title: if position matters!
learn_cards.body:
[expr for x in seq if cond] — filter (skip items)
  [expr_if_true if cond else expr_if_false for x in seq] — transform all items

learn_cards.code:
# Get unique first letters
names = ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "Anna", "Brian"]
first_letters = {name[0] for name in names}
print(first_letters)  # Duplicates removed automatically

# Flatten a 2D list
matrix = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]
flat = [num for row in matrix for num in row]
print(flat)

# Create a multiplication table
table = {(i, j): i * j for i in range(1, 4) for j in range(1, 4)}
for (i, j), product in table.items():
    print(f"  {i} x {j} = {product}")

lessons.title: Error Handling (try/except)
lessons.summary: Programs crash when they hit unexpected situations — dividing by zero, missing files, bad user input. Error handling lets you catch these problems gracefully instead of crashing.
checkpoint_titles: Full Pattern: try / except / else / finally

learn_cards.title: Why handle errors?
learn_cards.body: Programs crash when they hit unexpected situations — dividing by zero, missing files, bad user input. Error handling lets you catch these problems gracefully instead of crashing.

learn_cards.title: Full Pattern: try / except / else / finally

learn_cards.code:
def read_number(text):
    try:
        num = int(text)
    except ValueError:
        print(f"  '{text}' is not a number")
    else:
        # Runs ONLY if try succeeded (no exception)
        print(f"  Successfully parsed: {num}")
    finally:
        # ALWAYS runs, whether error or not
        print(f"  Done processing '{text}'")

read_number("42")
print()
read_number("abc")
learn_cards.output:
Successfully parsed: 42
  Done processing '42'

  'abc' is not a number
  Done processing 'abc'

learn_cards.title: else vs finally
learn_cards.body: else: runs only if no exception occurred. finally: ALWAYS runs — good for cleanup (closing files, connections).

lessons.title: File I/O (files, JSON, CSV)
lessons.summary: Python can read from and write to files on disk. The 'open()' function is the gateway. Always close files when done — or better, use 'with' to handle it automatically.

learn_cards.title: File I/O
learn_cards.body: Python can read from and write to files on disk. The 'open()' function is the gateway. Always close files when done — or better, use 'with' to handle it automatically.

learn_cards.title: Why 'with'?
learn_cards.body: The 'with' statement automatically closes the file when the block ends, even if an error occurs. This prevents resource leaks. Always use 'with' instead of manual open()/close().

learn_cards.code:
# Writing to a file
with open("example.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Hello, File!\n")
    f.write("Line 2\n")
# File is automatically closed here

# Reading the file
with open("example.txt", "r") as f:
    content = f.read()
    print(content)

# read() — entire file as one string
with open("example.txt") as f:
    all_text = f.read()

# readline() — one line at a time
with open("example.txt") as f:
    first_line = f.readline()  # "Hello, File!\n"

# readlines() — list of all lines
with open("example.txt") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()  # ["Hello, File!\n", "Line 2\n"]

# Best: iterate directly (memory-efficient)
with open("example.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip())  # strip() removes \n

learn_cards.title: JSON
learn_cards.body: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the standard format for data exchange. Python's json module converts between Python dicts/lists and JSON strings.

learn_cards.code:
import json

# Python dict -> JSON string
data = {"name": "Aniketh", "skills": ["Python", "Java"], "age": 25}
json_str = json.dumps(data, indent=2)
print(json_str)

# JSON string -> Python dict
parsed = json.loads(json_str)
print(f"Name: {parsed['name']}")

# Write JSON to file
with open("data.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(data, f, indent=2)

# Read JSON from file
with open("data.json") as f:
    loaded = json.load(f)
    print(f"Loaded: {loaded}")

import csv

# Write CSV
with open("people.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["name", "age", "role"])
    writer.writerow(["Aniketh", 25, "Engineer"])
    writer.writerow(["Alice", 30, "Manager"])

# Read CSV
with open("people.csv") as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    for row in reader:
        print(f"  {row['name']} is {row['age']}")

lessons.title: Decorators & Closures
lessons.summary: In Python, functions are objects. You can assign them to variables, pass them as arguments, and return them from other functions. This is the foundation of decorators.

learn_cards.title: First-class functions
learn_cards.body: In Python, functions are objects. You can assign them to variables, pass them as arguments, and return them from other functions. This is the foundation of decorators.

learn_cards.title: Closures
learn_cards.body: A closure is a function that remembers variables from its enclosing scope, even after that scope has finished executing. The inner function 'closes over' the outer variables.

learn_cards.code:
def make_multiplier(factor):
    def multiply(x):
        return x * factor  # Remembers 'factor' from outer scope
    return multiply

double = make_multiplier(2)
triple = make_multiplier(3)

print(double(5))   # 10
print(triple(5))   # 15
print(double(10))  # 20

learn_cards.title: What is a decorator?
learn_cards.body: A decorator is a function that takes a function, adds some behavior, and returns a new function. The @decorator syntax is syntactic sugar for: func = decorator(func).

learn_cards.code:
import time

def timer(func):
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        start = time.time()
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        elapsed = time.time() - start
        print(f"  {func.__name__} took {elapsed:.4f}s")
        return result
    return wrapper

@timer  # Same as: slow_add = timer(slow_add)
def slow_add(a, b):
    time.sleep(0.1)
    return a + b

result = slow_add(3, 4)
print(f"  Result: {result}")

learn_cards.title: Why functools.wraps?
learn_cards.body: Without @wraps, the decorated function loses its original name and docstring. @wraps copies the original function's metadata to the wrapper.

Hello!
hello
Says hello.
